# 自然·环境·动植物 {.unnumbered}



> 本主题共 10 篇语境短文。每篇把一批旧词织进一个场景；目标词**加粗**，展开"本篇生词"可遮释义自测。



### A Walk Through Living and Dying Landscapes

The mountain trail begins where three paths converge at an old fire pit, its **ash** still faintly warm from the previous night. On either side of the path, tight **bud**s push through the soil — the first green fists of spring punching out of last season's **rot**. A **tit** lands on a branch above, tilting its head at a patch of **alga** clinging to the damp stone wall beside the stream. Somewhere deeper in the **dell**, a **cock** calls before the sun has fully cleared the ridge, and a **hawk** answers nothing, only banks silently on a thermal and disappears over the **tor**.

Down by the water the world grows stranger. An **eel** threads between the rocks, its body a slow ribbon of muscle. A cloud of **brit** drifts near the surface, and a duck dips her **beak** into the shallows, scooping them up. Her **pug**-faced rival — a broad, flat-nosed drake — **bark**s at a **pup** that has waded too deep. The **pup** yelps, scrambles back to the bank, and shakes **dust** from its fur. A **flea** leaps from the wet coat onto a clump of dried **hemp** stalks at the water's edge. Overhead, bees **buzz** through the **fowl**-yard flowers beyond the fence, where a **cow** stands chewing, indifferent to everything.

The trail climbs toward **firn** country, where snow compacts into something harder than memory. Up here the land is **arid** and bare; only a smear of **alga** on the leeward face of each boulder proves that life is still trying. The sun hangs like a copper **orb** behind thin cloud. A **mew** drifts from a gull circling the snowfield. Far below, a **fin** slices the glacial lake — a trout, maybe, or something older. In the cold air the **hump** of the ridge ahead looks almost animal, and the wind in the **bark** of the lone pine near the summit sounds, briefly, like something answering back.

### A Morning in the Wild Margin

The sun had barely cleared the **peak** when I set out along the field's edge. The dew still clung to the **lawn** beside the old farmhouse, and clumps of **iris** stood upright against the fence, their violet tongues catching the light. A little further on, **lily** flowers hung in loose bells over the bank of a **brook** that chattered through the meadow. Tangles of **vine** and **ferns** draped the stone wall behind them, and a lone **daisy** had pushed up through a crack in the mortar.

I followed the water into wetter ground. The path grew soft underfoot—almost a **mire**—and I watched where I stepped. A **newt** slid off a mossy rock into the shallows, leaving the faintest ripple. Somewhere in the mud a **mole** had been busy: fresh casts dotted the bank like small volcanos. On the far side of the **creek**, a knot of **cacti** had escaped some garden and taken hold on the dry gravel slope above the flood line. A **slug** traced a silver thread across a dock leaf, unhurried and indifferent. A **tern** cut low overhead, banked hard, and was gone.

The **brant** were grazing the stubble field beyond the hedge—fifteen or twenty birds, heads down among last year's **crops**. A small herd of **bison** stood further back, massive and still, their breath steaming. A **chimp** would have found this landscape unreadable, but the animals here seemed wholly at ease. Near the water's edge I could see where a **cisco** had jumped: a silver arc, then nothing. A **bunny** bolted from the **weed**s I disturbed; the green **stem** of a reed snapped back after it passed. Something in the air carried an **odor**—not **olid** exactly, just rich, fermented, alive. I noticed a **tick** had attached itself to my sleeve and flicked it away. In the mud I found the broad gouge of a **tusk**, probably a feral pig rooting through the night. The **pest** damage to the reed bed was obvious: whole stands bent and broken.

A **bison** bull lifted his head as I passed. Above the tree line, a pair of **tern**s rode a thermal toward the summit. I checked the **fauna** list in my notebook, added **brant**, and turned back. The brook was still talking. The **iris** glowed. The morning held.

### A Walk Through Living Land

At dawn, a **flock** of geese crosses the sky above a **taiga** where spruce and larch crowd the horizon. Below the canopy, the **flora** is sparse but stubborn: patches of **pansy** push through the duff, their purple **petal**s trembling in a cold draft that carries the resinous **scent** of pine. Further south, a fringe of **grove**s gives way to open ground, and the soil shifts — dark **humus** packed over pale **loess** — as the land gradually descends toward water.

A **marsh** opens at the forest's edge, and beside it a wider **swamp** where black **slime** coats every root. **Spawn** drifts in cloudy ribbons through the shallows; **guppy**-like fry dart among them. A **snail** inches along a reed stem, indifferent to the **leech** gliding just beneath the surface. On a low **mound** of **mulch**ed leaves, a gardener has scattered handfuls of rye **grain** to attract birds, and the wet earth around it is dimpled with **moose** tracks from the night before.

By midday the light reaches the **shore** of a small cove. A tidal pool cradles one pale **pearl** of a quartz pebble among the rocks, and a **ridge** of sea-grass marks the tide line. A **pussy**willow branch, dropped by some upstream **pooch**'s enthusiastic retrieval, bobs at the water's edge. Farther inland, past the **polar** cold of shadow, a child photographs the amber beads of **myrrh** oozing from a trunk while bees **swarm** over the **pampa**-grass plumes at the clearing's border. At dusk a **pooch** startles a **moose** on the ridge path — the great animal disappearing into the **grove** with the calm certainty of something that has always belonged here.

### A Walk Through Wilderness and Wetland

The old trail wound through a **marshy** depression where every reed and rotting log wore a sleeve of **cobweb**, silver with morning dew. A **collie** that had followed us from the farm sniffed at a dried **cocoon** lodged in the bark of a fallen **trunk**, then bounded ahead into the sedge. Along the bank, a **beaver** had been at work all night: fresh white chips lay scattered like **flakes** of bone across the mud, and a neat dam backed the stream into a dark pool where **trout** nosed the current beneath a low **canopy** of willow.

Further on, the path crossed a broad **tract** of open grassland — **barren** in patches where **locust** swarms had stripped it bare two summers back. Among the surviving stems, **canola** had seeded itself in bright-yellow drifts, and a stand of **tulip** poplars marked where the soil deepened again. A **castor**-oil plant sprawled at the field's edge, its broad leaves sheltering a **fungus** the colour of rust. We watched a **gadfly** trace erratic loops above the **bovine** indifference of two grazing cattle, while a **kitten** from the nearby farmhouse stalked something invisible through the grass with murderous patience.

The forest resumed at the ridge. Beneath a **laurel** thicket, **irides** were just opening — their falls veined like the wing of a **bonobo**'s eye in a wildlife photograph I once saw. A newly **fledge**d crow tested its wings from a low branch, knocking loose a **thorn** from the bramble below. Deeper in the shade, an **iguana**-green log turned out to be a log at all — just the slow fantasy of **fossil** light filtering through leaves. A **mammal**'s footprint, too wide for a **coyote** and too round for a dog, pressed into the soft earth beside a root. Above the whole scene, the tree-tops opened just enough to show the late-afternoon **galaxy** of midges spiralling in a shaft of gold, a private **gemini** of light and shadow that no **tract** on botany had ever managed to describe.

### Where the Wild World Breathes

Just beyond the old **stable**, a broad **meadow** stretches toward the tree line, its grasses peppered with **yarrow** in full white bloom and dotted with **pollen**-heavy **shrubs** that **ramify** outward in every direction, sending thin branches across the footpath. **Mosses** carpet the shaded banks of a slow creek, cushioning every **pebble** in the shallows, while clumps of **totora** reed stand tall at the water's edge, their roots anchoring the **swampy** margin against erosion. A **wattle** fence, woven from green branches, borders the far end of the field — beyond it the land rises into long **ridges** that catch the afternoon light.

The animal life here is generous and unhurried. A **pigeon** murmurs from the eaves of the barn, a **pecker** works methodically up a dead oak, and a pair of **ravens** trade calls across the canopy. High overhead, a **raptor** turns slow circles, reading thermals. Nearer the ground, a **parrot** escaped from some garden long ago has made itself at home among the flowering **shrubs**. Down at the creek's edge, a family of **skunks** picks through the leaf litter, indifferent to the **urchin**-like toddler watching from a safe distance. A **sponge** of damp earth at the water line releases **spores** with every footfall, the invisible dust of next season's ferns already dispersing on the breeze. A fox slips past the collapsed **pigsty** at the field's south corner without breaking stride.

Not everything here is alive with ease. Where the creek bends, a slow seep of **sewage** from an upstream farm has left a band of grey **sludge** along the bank, and the vegetation there has begun to **wither** — stems gone papery, color drained. Only the most stubborn survivors hold on: a few tufts of grass rooted in what might once have been **mundic**-flecked spoil from an old mine working, their tips still green. Far from this damaged strip, the **pampas** grasses on the open slope move like water in the wind, and in the cooling dusk the first **meteor** arcs silently overhead, burning out long before it reaches the **tundra** country to the north, where the stars will soon arrange themselves into the ghostly shape of a **nebula** no city-dweller ever sees.

### A Day Between Root and Sky

The valley woke slowly. From its **bedrock** foundation of pale **granite**, a seep fed upward through every **crevice** in the stone, filling the **aquifer** below the meadow where **alfalfa** swayed in dense rows. Stands of **birches** lined the creek bank, their white bark bright against a row of **cypress** darkening the far edge. **Daisies** dotted the grass between them, and by the water a patch of **anemone** nodded in the current of air. **Jasmine** had climbed the fence post nearest the old **beehive**, filling the morning with sweetness the bees found without any effort at all.

The **climate** here was kind, and the soil **fertile**. **Insects** moved through the clover in slow purposeful arcs. A **lizards**-quick shadow crossed the warm rock — one of several that sunned themselves near the **lichens** crusting the north face. Upstream, a **catfish** held still in a pool where a small **cascade** tumbled over mossy stones and the water ran cold enough to sting. A **fledged** kingfisher sat on a branch above it, wholly serious.

Further out, on the open plain, a **gazelle** lifted its head. A **leopard** watched from a low branch of the acacia, motionless. Farther still, a **giraffe** moved between trees at its unhurried angle. In the coastal hills beyond the plain, a researcher photographed a **gorilla** family feeding in the understory, recorded a **dolphin** pod rounding the headland, and noted fresh evidence of **goonies** nesting on the cliff. Back at camp, her **hamster** turned its wheel in the equipment tent. On the horizon, one remaining **iceberg** caught the afternoon sun and sent a slow **calving** crack across the silence. A **carcass** of a whale had beached below it weeks before, and the **blubber** was still drawing scavengers from miles around.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### A Day Spent Reading the Living Land

The old **barnyard** stirred before dawn. A **rooster** crowed from the fence post, his call rolling out across the **meadows** where dew still pearled on every blade. Beyond the **paddock**, a **Labrador** nosed along the hedgerow, flushing a **raccoon** that had been raiding the compost heap — and with it, a writhing cluster of pale **maggots** the dog wisely left alone. Under the eaves, a colony of **termite**s had been quietly hollowing a beam all summer, their work as patient as the seasons.

The path led uphill through a grove of towering **sequoia**s, their bark the colour of dried blood, their roots threading through soil kept damp by **climatic** patterns older than any map. **Conifers** crowded the ridge beyond, releasing a sharp, **fragrant** resin that mixed with the fainter sweetness of a **camellia** hedge below. Near the stone wall, **daffodil**s and **geranium**s shared a narrow bed, and a stray sprig of **fumewort** pushed between the **pebbles** of the path. A tangle of **cannabis**-family weeds clung to the wire fence, half-smothered by last year's growth.

Lower down, a pond held its own small cosmos. **Tadpole**s hung in the shallows, gills still visible, while **rotifer**s turned invisible wheels in the deeper water. The muddy bank was thick with **bivalves**, and one could just make out the **piscine** shadows of small carp threading between the reeds. A stray **penguin** illustration on the park's information board reminded visitors that the **volcano** visible on the horizon once sent ash as far as the southern ice shelf — a humbling footnote on how little separates one **climatic** age from the next. A **peacock** from the estate next door picked its way across the wet grass, ignoring a **terrier** that bounced and barked at its tail. Overhead, **gazelle**-shaped clouds dissolved in the wind. Someone had pinned a note to the **farmland** gate: *Please **conserve** water — **hatching** season underway.*

### A Walk Through Living Worlds

At the edge of the **vineyard**, where rows of grapevines give way to tangled scrub, the morning light turned **lavender** over the hills. A lone **squirrel** flickered between the **deciduous** oaks, cheeks full, racing to squirrel its cache away before the season turned. Underfoot, **dandelion** clocks trembled in the breeze, and a cluster of **carnation** blooms blazed pink along the low stone wall. Further out, past the tended rows, the land slipped into open **chaparral** — dry, silver-grey **bluegrass** brushing against shin-height shrubs. Somewhere in the tangle, a **chameleon** froze on a branch, skin shifting to match the mottled bark, while nearby a **cockroach** vanished into the root litter.

The creek below told a different story. A **mangrove** thicket clung to the brackish shallows, its arching roots half-submerged, offering shelter to every small **organism** willing to squeeze through. A **tortoise** eased along the muddy bank, unhurried. Out in the current, a **stingray** glided low over the sand, and a pair of **porpoise** rolled beyond the mouth of the inlet, their backs catching the **sapphire** glint of open water. This stretch had stayed **pristine** — no runoff, no sprawl — and the **fecundity** of the place showed in everything: the layered canopy, the crowded shallows, the constant movement.

Not all relationships here were gentle. A **venomous** snake lay coiled beneath a **magnolia**, watching. The tree itself hosted a silent community: **termites** worked the heartwood, a **parasite** vine coiled its tendrils up the bark, and a **symbiote** fungus threaded through the roots below, trading minerals for sugars in the dark. A **carnivore** — a hawk, perched high — watched a stand of **milkweed** where monarchs clustered. It was waiting, as all **predator**s wait, for the one moment of inattention. High on the ridge, a slab of **obsidian** jutted from the cliff face, smooth and ancient, left behind when long-dead seas receded and **ammonoids** turned to stone in the limestone below it. Above, a cornice of old snow hung heavy — one warm afternoon away from becoming an **avalanche** that would reshape the slope entirely, the way the living world always does, slowly and then all at once.

### A Morning Walk Through Living and Vanishing Worlds

The valley had remarkable **fertility** — dark loam banked against ridges of **sandstone**, carved over millennia by the slow logic of **tectonics**. Geologists still argued about the **deposition** layers exposed along the eastern cliff: bands of chalky **cretaceous** rock sandwiched between iron-rich seams of **magnetite**. Somewhere above those seams, a **meteorite** had left a thin, dark line in the strata — a calling card from deep time, when **megafauna** still roamed and every **angiosperm** was a new experiment.

By mid-morning the scrub came alive. A lone **herbivore** — a mule deer — moved through a stand of **sagebrush**, pausing to nose at a fallen **pine cone**. Overhead, a **budgerigar** escaped from some distant homestead flashed green against the sky, improbable beside a native **sandpiper** picking its way along the mudflat. Near the water's edge, **quicksand** made the ground treacherous; a sign warned walkers off the soft margin. Out beyond the surf break, a solitary **swordfish** finned through the chop, and a **bluebottle** jellyfish drifted just beneath the surface like a bruise in the water. Farther inland, in the humid canyon, someone had planted a **heliotrope** against a stone wall, its purple clusters tracking the sun.

The afternoon revealed subtler dramas. Bright strands of **mistletoe** hung from an oak — **parasitic**, yes, yet part of a larger web: the berries fed the **fledgling** thrushes just learning flight. That web was **ecological** **mutualism** at its most visible, one organism's cost becoming another's advantage. A research station at the trailhead displayed jars of minerals and bones: a **vestigial** hind-limb from a whale, a tank holding a sleepy lizard mid-**estivation**, and behind glass, a scale model of the historic **menagerie** that once occupied these grounds before the **orangutan** enclosure was dismantled. Outside, a bin labeled **recycling** stood beside a panel explaining why the valley's shale held no viable **petroleum** — and why that, in the long run, was the luckiest thing that ever happened to it.

### Wandering the Wild: From Deep Earth to Treetop

The trail began at the edge of **timberland**, where centuries-old conifers rose from **stratified** layers of rock and soil — a visible record of the slow forces that had shaped the valley. Geologists had mapped the ridge above as a **subduction** zone, and its gradual **subsidence** had left the creek bed lower every decade. Underfoot, last autumn's **chrysanthemum** stalks lay pressed into the mud beside sprays of **meadowsweet** and clumps of **willow-herb**, all working their way back into the earth through the quiet chemistry of **biodegradable** decay.

A **conservationist** from the regional trust had spent the morning cataloguing **pollination** patterns in the old **plantation** downstream, where introduced flowering species were drawing native bees away from the surrounding meadow. She paused to watch a **mockingbird** run through its borrowed repertoire overhead, then crouched to photograph a **salamander** half-hidden under a mossy shelf of stone. Nearby, an **invertebrate** survey had turned up rare aquatic larvae — small proof that **contamination** levels in the feeder stream had finally begun to fall.

The afternoon light caught a display board the trust had installed near the trailhead. It traced the deep history of animal diet and behavior: an artist's reconstruction of **Ambulocetus**, the ancient walking whale, suggested an **omnivorous** early phase before full marine **domestication** of a body plan; a panel on **herbivorous** browsers showed how grazing shaped entire landscapes; another explained **parasitism** among woodland fungi, noting that the damp walls of the equipment shed had developed their own **domestic fungus** colony. A diagram of **plate tectonics** framed it all, reminding visitors that the meadow they stood in had once been seafloor. A small exhibit on **archaeopteryx** anchored the evolutionary arc from feathered theropod to the birds calling above, while a tank of **Poeciliidae** — small, adaptable livebearers — illustrated adaptive radiation in miniature. The board ended with a gentle pitch for **back-to-nature** education programs, urging a culture less indifferent to the **hingganite**-bearing outcrops and the ten thousand ordinary miracles surrounding them.
